title: Rachel's plea (Lamentations Rabbah, Proem 24)
hookLine: after the Temple falls, the patriarchs plead; only Rachel's plea is answered
tomorrow: the Temple is rubble. what do you bring now instead?

cards: A group chat often has an order nobody says out loud: whose message gets a reply first. Keep that in mind, because a midrash on Lamentations has the strangest reply order in the Bible. The Temple has fallen.
The people are being led away. Abraham pleads with God. No answer.
Isaac pleads. Jacob pleads. Then Moses, the man who talked God out of anger in the desert.
Silence. Then Rachel speaks: not a founding father, not a lawgiver, the younger sister from Genesis. And she's the one God answers.

teach.b: Her plea is a story about herself. Rachel says: Jacob worked for years to marry me, and on the wedding night my father planned to send my sister Leah in my place. I knew.
I could have exposed it. Instead, so Leah wouldn't be shamed, I helped her through it; the midrash says she even gave her sister the signs she and Jacob had agreed on. Then comes the argument.

teach.h: I WAS NOT JEALOUS. WHY ARE YOU?
teach.b: I, flesh and blood, was not jealous of my rival. So why are You jealous of idols that are nothing? And God's mercy is stirred: for your sake, Rachel, I will bring them back.
The midrash hangs it on Jeremiah, who hears "Rachel weeping for her children," and then the promise that they will come home. So, the puzzle solved. The fathers plead from what they did for God.
Rachel pleads from what she gave up for someone else, the hardest thing: her sister in her place. She doesn't argue rules.
She shows the mercy she's asking for. One to tell a friend tonight: in this midrash, the voice heaven answers isn't the greatest prophet.
It's a sister who wasn't jealous. And notice who she asks for. Not herself.

how: Jeremiah's verse of Rachel weeping for her children is read in synagogue on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, and prayers for the sick are said for them by name.

o: a protest Rachel made against her sister Leah
a plea for others, made from mercy already shown
a prayer Rachel wrote for her own lost child

games.q: who pleads, and how — tap the pairs.
p: pleads from mercy she already showed
the sister Rachel refused to shame
hears Rachel weeping for her children

s: God answers Rachel because she cries the loudest
she's answered for her mercy: I was not jealous of my rival, so why are You jealous?
in the midrash, Abraham and Moses plead before Rachel does
the fathers and Moses plead first and meet silence; then Rachel speaks.
she pleads for her children, the people being led away long after her.

games.q: two friends of yours are in a fight, and you want one to let it go. what would asking in Rachel's way sound like?
o: "I let one go once, when it cost me. could you try it too?"
"here are all the reasons she deserves another chance."
"if you two don't make up, I'll be the one who's hurt."
games.why: Rachel asked for mercy by pointing to her own: I wasn't jealous of my rival. the plea that's heard is made from mercy already shown.

practice: Bring to mind one person who needs someone to speak up for them: a friend waiting on news, a sibling in trouble, a neighbor stuck in a hard month.

On paper, by hand, write one sentence you could say on their behalf to whoever could help. If you pray, you can hold them the way Rachel held her children; if not, keep the sentence where you'll see it.

wordCard.voice: Rachel's plea: the one the midrash says God answered, made for her children, from a mercy she had already shown her sister.

orig.note: Hebrew: Rachel, the matriarch Jeremiah hears weeping for her children.

carryVoice: Hold on to this one: rachel's plea, asked for someone else. Day thirty-one of reading midrash.

sources.ref: Lamentations Rabbah, Proem (Petichta) 24 (the patriarchs and Moses plead; Rachel recalls sparing Leah; God's mercy is stirred)
Jeremiah 31:16–17 (the promise that the children will come back)
Genesis 29:15–30 (Jacob works for Rachel; Laban gives Leah on the wedding night)
